content: In combinatorial mathematics, a block design, more formally known as a balanced incomplete block design, is a specific type of set system. It has significant applications in experimental design, a branch of statistics, as well as in purely combinatorial contexts. Consider a finite set ( X ), whose elements are referred to as points, and integers ( k ), ( r ), and ( lambda ), all greater than or equal to 1. A 2-design ( B ) is defined as a collection of ( k )-element subsets of ( X ), called blocks, such that the following conditions are satisfied: 1. The number ( r ) of blocks containing any given point ( x ) in ( X ) is the same for all points ( x ). 2. The number ( lambda ) of blocks containing any pair of distinct points ( x ) and ( y ) in ( X ) is also independent of the choice of ( x ) and ( y ). The parameters of the design are denoted as ( v ) (the number of elements in ( X ), referred to as points), ( b ) (the number of blocks), ( k ), ( r ), and ( lambda ). Importantly, ( B ) does not necessarily include all possible ( k )-element subsets of ( X ); this is the meaning of the term incomplete. Such a design is referred to as a ( (v, k, lambda) )-design or a ( (v, b, r, k, lambda) )-design. The parameters ( v ), ( k ), and ( lambda ) determine ( b ) and ( r ), and not all combinations of ( v ), ( k ), and ( lambda ) are feasible. Two fundamental equations connect these parameters. A key theorem, known as Fisher's inequality, states that ( b geq v ) in any block design. When equality holds (( b = v )), the design is called a symmetric design, which possesses several unique properties. Examples of block designs include: The lines in finite projective planes, where ( X ) is the set of points in the plane and ( lambda = 1 ). This is a relatively simple example of a symmetric design. Steiner triple systems, where ( k = 3 ). A generalization of block designs is the concept of ( t )-designs. For any integer ( t geq 2 ), a ( t )-design ( B ) is a collection of ( k )-element subsets of ( X ), called blocks, such that: 1. The number ( r ) of blocks containing any given point ( x ) in ( X ) is independent of ( x ). 2. The number ( lambda ) of blocks containing any given ( t )-element subset ( T ) of ( X ) is independent of the choice of ( T ). The parameters of a ( t )-design are ( v ) (the number of elements in ( X )), ( b ) (the number of blocks), ( k ), ( r ), ( lambda ), and ( t ). Such a design is referred to as a ( t )-(v, k, (lambda))-design. These parameters determine ( b ) and ( r ), and the values of ( v ), ( k ), ( lambda ), and ( t ) cannot be chosen arbitrarily. The equations governing these parameters involve ( b_i ), the number of blocks containing any ( i )-element subset of points. An example of a ( t )-design is the ( d )-dimensional subspaces of a finite projective geometry, where ( t = d + 1 ) and ( lambda = 1 ). The term block design typically refers to a 2-design unless otherwise specified.
